OVERVIEW.detail: A single-page browser game where players slide and merge numbered tiles on a 4×4 grid to reach 2048. One unified JS component handles grid logic, rendering, input, scoring, and local storage.

boxes.label: Playing 2048
boxes.sub: Slide and merge tiles to reach 2048

explain.body: 2048 is a browser-based sliding puzzle game where a player merges numbered tiles on a 4×4 grid, aiming to create a tile with the value 2048. It runs entirely client-side with no server — just HTML, CSS, and plain JavaScript. A **GameManager** orchestrates each turn: it listens for arrow-key or swipe input through a **KeyboardInputManager**, updates a **Grid** of **Tile** objects by sliding and merging them, then tells an **HTMLActuator** to redraw the board and a **LocalStorageManager** to save the score and grid state. On page load, `application.js` wires these four components together, and the game is ready. The core loop is: receive a direction → traverse the grid in that direction → shift every tile as far as it can go, merging same-valued neighbors → spawn a random new tile → check for win or loss → actuate (render and persist).

glossary.meaning: Central controller that owns the grid, processes each move, spawns tiles, and delegates rendering and storage.
A 4×4 two-dimensional array of cell positions that stores Tile references and supports traversal and availability queries.
An object holding a numeric value and its current and previous positions, capable of merging with an equal-valued neighbor.
Listens for keyboard arrow keys, touch swipes, and button clicks, then fires directional move or restart events.
Reads game state and writes it into the DOM — adds tile elements, updates the score display, and shows win or lose messages.
Persists and retrieves the current game state, best score, and grid snapshot using the browser's localStorage API.
The step where the GameManager sends the full grid and score metadata to the HTMLActuator for rendering.
Walk through grid cells in a direction-dependent order so tiles slide and merge correctly from farthest to nearest.
When two tiles of equal value collide, they combine into one tile whose value is their sum, adding to the score.

children.sub: Initializes the game and wires components
children.detail: `GameManager` is instantiated in `application.js` with grid size 4 and freshly constructed `KeyboardInputManager`, `HTMLActuator`, and `LocalStorageManager` instances, triggering the first render via `requestAnimationFrame`.

code.label: Entry point that initializes the 2048 game with a 4x4 grid and wires up input, rendering, and storage managers.

children.detail: Defers game construction until the first animation frame via `requestAnimationFrame`, then instantiates `GameManager` with a size-4 grid and the three manager classes.

explain.body: This is the single entry point for the whole game. It waits for the browser to signal it is ready to draw (using `requestAnimationFrame`, a browser API that calls your code just before the next screen refresh), then creates the central `GameManager` object that connects input, display, and save-state together.

rows.title: Wait for paint-ready frame
rows.detail: `window.requestAnimationFrame` delays execution until the browser is ready to render, avoiding visual glitches on load.

rows.title: Instantiate GameManager
rows.detail: `new GameManager(4, KeyboardInputManager, HTMLActuator, LocalStorageManager)` wires together the full game with a 4×4 grid.

explain.body: When the page loads, the game needs a single place that creates all the pieces and connects them. This entry point builds the four main objects — the game logic controller, the input listener, the screen renderer, and the save/load manager — and hands the last three into the controller. Think of it as the ignition key: it doesn't contain game rules itself, but without it nothing starts. The grid size (4×4) is set here, making it the only place you'd change the board dimensions.

children.title: Game Controller
children.sub: Orchestrates grid, moves, scoring, and persistence
children.detail: The `GameManager` constructor wires input handlers, initializes or restores grid state via storage, and exposes methods for moves, scoring, and win/loss checks. `getVector` translates a direction code (0–3) into an {x, y} offset vector used by the move logic.

Saves game state to storage and updates the actuator with current grid and metadata

children.title: Game Control
children.sub: Runs all game logic from setup through win
children.detail: Coordinates tile movement, merging, scoring, win/loss detection, and state persistence through `move`, `actuate`, `serialize`, and related methods on `GameManager`.

explain.body: This is the brain of the game. It listens for the player's directional input, works out which tiles can slide and which pairs can merge (two tiles of equal value touching in the move direction combine into one doubled tile), updates the score, checks whether the player has reached 2048 or run out of moves, and tells both the display and the save system about every change.

rows.title: Wire up managers and events
rows.detail: The constructor instantiates `InputManager`, `StorageManager`, and `Actuator`, then binds `move`, `restart`, and `keepPlaying` events to their handlers.

rows.title: Restore or create game state
rows.detail: `setup` calls `storageManager.getGameState()`; if a saved state exists it rebuilds `Grid` and flags from it, otherwise creates a fresh grid and calls `addStartTiles`.

rows.title: Place opening tiles
rows.detail: `addStartTiles` loops `startTiles` times calling `addRandomTile`, which picks a random empty cell and places a tile with value 2 (90 % chance) or 4.

rows.title: Persist and render state
rows.detail: `actuate` updates the best score, saves or clears game state via `storageManager`, then calls `actuator.actuate` with the grid and metadata.

rows.title: Slide and merge tiles
rows.detail: `move` builds a traversal order via `buildTraversals`, slides each tile to its `findFarthestPosition`, merges equal-value neighbours, adds a random tile, and sets `this.over` if `movesAvailable` returns false.

children.title: Move Helpers
children.sub: Translates direction codes into grid traversal logic
children.detail: Converts a direction integer to an x/y delta via `getVector`, builds correct traversal order via `buildTraversals`, slides a tile to its farthest open cell via `findFarthestPosition`, and checks remaining moves via `tileMatchesAvailable`.

explain.body: These helpers answer two questions the game logic needs: 'where does this tile end up if I slide it?' and 'is there any move left at all?' By converting directions to numeric deltas first, the same sliding code works identically for all four directions without special cases.

rows.title: Direction to vector
rows.detail: `getVector` maps the direction integer (0–3) to a unit x/y delta so movement calculations are direction-agnostic.

rows.title: Build traversal order
rows.detail: `buildTraversals` builds 0-to-size index arrays then reverses the axis whose vector is positive so tiles are always processed farthest-first.

rows.title: Find slide destination
rows.detail: `findFarthestPosition` steps a cell one unit at a time along the vector until it hits a wall or occupied cell, returning the last free position and the first blocked cell.

rows.title: Check for remaining merges
rows.detail: `tileMatchesAvailable` scans every tile in all four directions; if any neighbour shares its value a move is still possible and it returns `true`.

explain.body: When you play 2048, something has to keep track of the board, react to every swipe or keypress, slide and merge tiles, update the score, and decide whether you've won or lost. This file is that "something." On startup it either loads a saved game from the browser's local storage or sets up a fresh 4×4 grid with two random tiles. Each time the player presses an arrow key or swipes, the manager figures out which direction that corresponds to—up, down, left, or right—translates it into a grid-coordinate offset (for example, "left" becomes x: −1, y: 0), then walks every tile in the correct order to slide and merge them. After each move it adds a new random tile, updates the score (bumping the best score if beaten), checks for a win (a 2048 tile) or a loss (no moves left), saves the new state back to storage, and tells the renderer to redraw the screen.

boxes.label: Game Control
boxes.sub: Runs all game logic from setup through win

boxes.label: Move Helpers
boxes.sub: Translates direction codes into grid traversal logic

explain.body: This is the brain of the game. When a player swipes or presses an arrow key, the controller must figure out what happens to every tile on the board. It walks each row or column in the direction of the move, sliding tiles as far as they can go and merging two tiles of equal value into one worth double. Each merge adds to the score. After every move it places a new random tile (value 2 or 4) on an empty cell. It then checks whether any tile has reached 2048 (a win) or whether no moves remain (a loss). Finally it saves the updated board and score to browser storage so progress survives a page refresh.

boxes.label: Game Controller
boxes.sub: Orchestrates grid, moves, scoring, and persistence

children.title: Controlling Input
children.sub: Captures keyboard, touch, and button events
children.detail: `KeyboardInputManager` binds keydown listeners mapping arrow/WASD/Vim keys to directions, tracks touchstart/touchend for swipe detection with a threshold, and listens for click events on retry/restart/keep-playing buttons, dispatching all through an `emit`/`on` event system.

code.label: Captures keyboard input, touch/swipe gestures, and button clicks to emit game control events.

children.title: Capture Input
children.sub: Turns keyboard, touch, and button events into game
children.detail: Listens for arrow/WASD/vim keys and touch swipes to `emit` a numbered direction, and binds retry/restart/keep-playing buttons to their respective events.

explain.body: Every way a player can control the game — keyboard arrow keys, the WASD or vim movement keys, tapping buttons on screen, or swiping on a touchscreen — is caught here and translated into a small set of named events ('move', 'restart', 'keepPlaying') that the game manager subscribes to. The `emit`/`on` pair is a minimal event bus built into this class.

rows.title: Detect pointer API
rows.detail: The constructor checks `window.navigator.msPointerEnabled` to pick the correct IE10 or standard touch event names before calling `listen`.

rows.title: Register keyboard handler
rows.detail: A `keydown` listener maps key codes (arrows, WASD, vim hjkl) to direction integers 0–3 and calls `emit('move', mapped)`, while key 82 triggers `restart`.

rows.title: Bind UI buttons
rows.detail: `bindButtonPress` attaches both `click` and touch-end listeners on `.retry-button`, `.restart-button`, and `.keep-playing-button` to their handler functions.

rows.title: Detect swipe direction
rows.detail: Touch start records coordinates; touch end computes dx/dy and, if the gesture exceeds 10 px, calls `emit('move', …)` with the dominant axis direction.

explain.body: Players interact with 2048 in several ways — arrow keys on a desktop, finger swipes on a phone, or clicking buttons to restart. This module listens for all of those and translates them into simple events the game controller understands. For touch input, it records where a finger lands and where it lifts off; if the distance exceeds a small threshold, it calculates the dominant direction (up, down, left, right) and fires a 'move' event. Keyboard presses are mapped from key codes to the same four directions. Button clicks fire 'restart' or 'keepPlaying' events. The game controller subscribes to these events without needing to know how input was captured.

boxes.label: Capture Input
boxes.sub: Turns keyboard, touch, and button events into game

children.title: Rendering Board
children.sub: Draws tiles, scores, and messages to DOM
children.detail: `HTMLActuator` clears the tile container each frame via `requestAnimationFrame`, then rebuilds tile elements with position/value CSS classes (including merge and new-tile animations), updates score counters with animated addition badges, and toggles game-over or win message overlays.

code.label: Renders game state to the DOM, updating tile display, score display, and game-over/win messages.

children.title: Render Board
children.sub: Writes game state to the DOM each turn
children.detail: On each call to `actuate`, clears and redraws all tiles via `addTile`, updates score counters via `updateScore`/`updateBestScore`, and shows win/loss messages via `message`.

explain.body: After every move the game manager calls this class to make the screen match the new state. It wipes the tile layer and redraws each tile at its new position, using CSS class names to trigger slide and pop animations. It also keeps the score counter up to date and flashes a 'You win!' or 'Game over!' overlay when the game ends.

rows.title: Clear and redraw tiles
rows.detail: `actuate` uses `requestAnimationFrame` to clear `.tile-container` then iterates `grid.cells`, calling `addTile` for each occupied cell.

rows.title: Build tile element with animation class
rows.detail: `addTile` creates a wrapper div, assigns CSS classes including position and value (e.g. `tile-4`, `tile-position-2-3`), then adds `tile-new`, `tile-merged`, or schedules a move animation via a nested `requestAnimationFrame`.

rows.title: Update score display
rows.detail: `updateScore` replaces the score container text and appends a temporary `+N` addition element when the score increases.

rows.title: Show end-game message
rows.detail: `message` adds `game-won` or `game-over` class to `.game-message` and sets its paragraph text; `clearMessage` removes both classes on continue.

explain.body: After every move the game state is just numbers in memory — this module makes it visible. It wipes the tile container and recreates a DOM element for each tile, assigning CSS classes that encode position (like 'tile-position-3-2') and value (like 'tile-128'). Tiles that just appeared get a 'tile-new' class for a pop-in animation; tiles born from a merge get 'tile-merged'. The score display doesn't just show the number — it briefly flashes the points gained as a floating '+N' badge. When the game ends it adds a message overlay saying 'Game over!' or 'You win!' with appropriate classes, letting CSS handle the visual transition.

boxes.label: Render Board
boxes.sub: Writes game state to the DOM each turn

children.title: Grid And Tiles
children.sub: Models the game board and tile data
children.detail: `Grid` maintains a 2D array of cells, provides `availableCells`, `randomAvailableCell`, `cellContent`, `insertTile`, `removeTile`, and `serialize`/`fromState` for persistence. `Tile` holds `position`, `value`, `previousPosition`, and `mergedFrom` for animation tracking.

code.label: Manages the 2D grid of tiles, including cell state, tile insertion/removal, and grid serialization.

children.title: Grid State
children.sub: Manages the 4×4 cell array and tile placement
children.detail: Provides `empty`/`fromState` construction, `insertTile`/`removeTile` mutation, `availableCells`/`randomAvailableCell` queries, and `serialize` for persistence.

explain.body: The grid is the game board — a 4×4 table of slots, each either empty or holding a tile. This class is the single source of truth for where every tile sits. All movement and merge code asks it which cells are free, reads tile values from it, and writes updated positions back into it. It can also export itself as plain JSON so the game can be saved and reloaded.

rows.title: Build or restore cell array
rows.detail: The constructor calls `empty` to create a null-filled 2D array, or `fromState` to reconstruct `Tile` objects from a saved state.

rows.title: Query available cells
rows.detail: `availableCells` uses `eachCell` to collect all null positions; `randomAvailableCell` picks one at random from that list.

rows.title: Read and write individual cells
rows.detail: `cellContent` returns the tile at a position (or null if out of bounds); `insertTile` and `removeTile` write and clear a cell by tile coordinates.

rows.title: Serialize for storage
rows.detail: `serialize` rebuilds the 2D array as plain objects by calling each tile's `serialize`, wrapping it with `size` for JSON persistence.

children.title: Tile Data
children.sub: Stores one tile's position, value, and merge history
children.detail: Defines the `Tile` constructor with x/y/value and merge metadata, plus `savePosition`, `updatePosition`, and `serialize` methods.

explain.body: Every numbered square on the board is one `Tile` instance. Beyond its number and position, it remembers where it was before the last move (so the CSS animation slides it from the right place) and which two tiles it was formed from if it was just created by a merge (so both source tiles can flash before disappearing).

rows.title: Initialise tile fields
rows.detail: The constructor sets `x`, `y`, `value` (defaulting to 2), and clears `previousPosition` and `mergedFrom` to null.

rows.title: Track position for animation
rows.detail: `savePosition` snapshots the current coordinates into `previousPosition` before a move, letting the renderer animate from the old spot.

rows.title: Update coordinates after move
rows.detail: `updatePosition` overwrites `x` and `y` with the new cell's coordinates after a slide or merge.

rows.title: Export for persistence
rows.detail: `serialize` returns a plain object with `position` and `value` suitable for JSON storage.

explain.body: The game needs a structured way to represent the board and the pieces on it. The Grid is a square two-dimensional array where each cell is either empty or holds a Tile. It can list all empty cells (needed when placing a new random tile), insert or remove tiles, and convert itself to and from a plain object for saving. A Tile knows its current position, its value (2, 4, 8, etc.), where it was before the last move (so the renderer can animate sliding), and whether it was just created by merging two other tiles (so the renderer can animate a merge pulse). Together they form the pure data layer with no knowledge of the screen or user input.

children.title: Browser Compatibility
children.sub: Polyfills and storage for older browsers
children.detail: `animframe_polyfill` shims `requestAnimationFrame`/`cancelAnimationFrame` with vendor prefixes or a 16ms `setTimeout` fallback. `bind_polyfill` adds `Function.prototype.bind`.

code.label: Provides fallback implementations of requestAnimationFrame and cancelAnimationFrame for browsers lacking native support.

children.title: Animation Timing
children.detail: Tries vendor-prefixed `webkit`/`moz` versions first, then falls back to a `setTimeout`-based implementation targeting ~60 fps by computing 16 ms intervals.

explain.body: `requestAnimationFrame` is the standard browser API for scheduling animation code to run just before the screen repaints. Older browsers either didn't support it or used a browser-specific prefixed name. This file ensures that whatever browser runs the game, calling `window.requestAnimationFrame` always works, falling back to a timer that fires roughly 60 times per second.

rows.title: Try vendor-prefixed versions
rows.detail: Iterates `['webkit', 'moz']` and assigns the first available prefixed `RequestAnimationFrame` to `window.requestAnimationFrame`.

rows.title: Fallback with setTimeout
rows.detail: If still undefined, defines `requestAnimationFrame` using `window.setTimeout` with a delay of `max(0, 16 − elapsed)` ms to approximate a 60 fps cadence.

rows.title: Polyfill cancel
rows.detail: If `cancelAnimationFrame` is missing, replaces it with a simple `clearTimeout` wrapper.

children.title: Bind Polyfill
children.detail: Conditionally defines `Function.prototype.bind` with a closure that captures the target context and uses `apply` to invoke the original function.

explain.body: `Function.prototype.bind` lets you lock a function's `this` value to a specific object so it still refers to the right thing when called later as a callback. Very old browsers lacked it. This file adds the missing method only when it is absent, so the rest of the code can call `.bind(this)` safely everywhere.

rows.title: Guard against native support
rows.detail: Uses the `||` short-circuit so the polyfill body only runs when `Function.prototype.bind` is not already defined.

rows.title: Return bound wrapper
rows.detail: Returns a function that normalises its argument to an array and calls `self.apply(target, args)`, preserving the bound context.

children.title: ClassList Polyfill
children.sub: Adds classList to elements in browsers without it
children.detail: Defines a `DOMTokenList` class with `add`, `remove`, `contains`, `toggle`, and `item` methods, then installs it as a getter on `HTMLElement.prototype.classList`.

explain.body: `classList` is the convenient browser API for adding and removing CSS class names on an element (e.g. `element.classList.add('game-over')`). Older browsers did not have it. This file builds a complete replacement backed by the element's plain `className` string, then installs it on every HTML element so the renderer and input manager can use it without caring about browser version.

rows.title: Early exit if supported
rows.detail: Returns immediately if `classList` already exists on `document.documentElement`, leaving the native implementation untouched.

rows.title: Define DOMTokenList
rows.detail: Constructs `DOMTokenList` by splitting the element's `className` string on whitespace and implementing `add`, `remove`, `contains`, `toggle`, and `toString` using `Array.prototype` methods.

rows.title: Attach as a property getter
rows.detail: `defineElementGetter` uses `Object.defineProperty` (or `__defineGetter__` as fallback) to wire `classList` onto `HTMLElement.prototype` so every element returns a fresh `DOMTokenList`.

children.title: Save State
children.sub: Persists best score and game state across sessions
children.detail: Uses `localStorage` when available (detected via a test write), falling back to an in-memory `fakeStorage` object, to get/set the best score and serialised game state.

explain.body: `localStorage` is a browser feature that stores small pieces of text even after the tab is closed. This class uses it to remember the player's best score ever and to save the current board so refreshing the page resumes mid-game. If the browser blocks `localStorage` (e.g. private mode on some browsers), it silently falls back to memory-only storage that lasts only for the current tab session.

rows.title: Define in-memory fallback
rows.detail: `window.fakeStorage` mirrors the `localStorage` API (`setItem`, `getItem`, `removeItem`, `clear`) using a plain `_data` object.

rows.title: Detect localStorage support
rows.detail: `localStorageSupported` tries a test write/remove inside a `try/catch`; returns `true` only if no exception is thrown, selecting the real or fake storage accordingly.

rows.title: Best score persistence
rows.detail: `getBestScore` reads the stored number (defaulting to 0) and `setBestScore` writes the new high score via the chosen storage backend.

rows.title: Game state persistence
rows.detail: `setGameState` JSON-serialises the full game object and stores it; `getGameState` parses it back; `clearGameState` removes it on game over or restart.

explain.body: Not every browser supports modern JavaScript APIs. This layer ensures the game runs everywhere by filling in missing features. If the browser lacks requestAnimationFrame (the standard way to schedule smooth screen updates), a polyfill substitutes vendor-specific versions or falls back to a simple timer. If Function.prototype.bind (used to lock a function's 'this' context) is missing, a replacement is provided. If classList (a convenient way to add/remove CSS classes from elements) isn't available, a full DOMTokenList implementation is injected. Finally, the storage manager wraps localStorage — the browser's key-value store for saving data between visits — and if that isn't available either, it uses a plain JavaScript object as temporary storage so the game still works within a single session.

boxes.sub: Adds classList to elements in browsers without it

boxes.sub: Persists best score and game state across sessions

explain.body: This section is the entire client-side 2048 game. The player sees a 4×4 grid of numbered tiles and slides them in four directions; matching tiles merge and double in value, and the goal is to create a tile worth 2048. Under the hood, six layers cooperate: an entry point wires everything together, a game controller owns the rules and scoring, an input module captures keys and swipes, a renderer paints tiles and scores into the page, data models represent the board and pieces, and polyfills ensure it all works on older browsers. State is saved to the browser's local storage so refreshing the page resumes where you left off. The architecture is event-driven — input fires events, the controller reacts, updates the model, then tells the renderer to redraw.
